input_signals.name: CapexIntoErodingMargins
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(capx, ppegt)), RANK(NEG(TREND(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), at), 5))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Heavy capital spending relative to the existing capital base is bad news only when the firm's multi-year gross-profitability trend is deteriorating, i.e. management is adding capacity into a declining-return business; capex by firms with improving unit economics reflects genuine opportunity.
input_signals.reasoning: The five-year trend in gross profit over assets is a slow-moving productivity measure, so pairing it with current capex intensity distinguishes expansion into rising returns on capital from empire-building in a decaying franchise. Ranking both legs makes the interaction monotone in "unproductive investment intensity." Neither leg alone identifies the mismatch between capital deployment and realized productivity.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( capx, ppegt ) ), rank( neg( trend( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), at ), 5 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ExternalFundingGapImmatureFirms
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), oancf), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(re, at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Investment that exceeds internally generated cash must be externally financed; this funding gap is most damaging for firms with little accumulated retained earnings, which have no proven history of self-funding profitable growth and face the harshest capital-market discipline.
input_signals.reasoning: The first leg is an economic investment-minus-internal-cash gap (capex plus acquisitions less operating cash flow), a direct investment x quality quantity rather than a raw growth rate. Retained earnings over assets proxies for cumulative profitability and self-funding capability, so the product targets externally financed expansion by structurally unprofitable firms. COALESCE treats unreported acquisitions as zero spend, the economically correct convention.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( add( capx, coalesce( aqc, 0 ) ), oancf ), at ) ), rank( neg( ratio( re, at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: InvestmentProductivityMismatch
input_signals.expression: SUB(RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent)), RANK(TREND(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), at), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters is not the level of investment or the level of productivity but the gap between them: firms whose capital spending rank far exceeds the rank of their gross-profitability trend are over-investing relative to the returns their operations are actually delivering, and they subsequently underperform.
input_signals.reasoning: Because investment enters positively and profitability improvement enters negatively, the long-short leg holds high-capex/improving-productivity firms against high-capex/deteriorating-productivity firms, cancelling much of the CMA and RMW loading that killed the alpha of the gen-0 rank-product version. The 3-year trend (rather than 5-year) also raises coverage materially. This isolates the interaction as a relative-mismatch concept rather than a double penalty.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( rank( ratio( capx, ppent ) ), rank( trend( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), at ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: IssuanceFundedGrowthMinusInternalCash
input_signals.expression: SUB(RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, DELTA(dltt, 1)), at)), RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Expansion financed by fresh equity and debt issuance rather than by durable internal cash generation is low-quality growth; the wedge between a firm's external-financing rank and its smoothed operating-cash-flow rank identifies firms whose asset base is being built with other people's money.
input_signals.reasoning: This keeps the mechanism that produced the archive's only reliable alpha (investment minus internal cash) but replaces the accounting-gap version with actual financing flows (sstk and debt issuance), which are timelier and better measured than aqc. Smoothing operating cash flow over three years separates persistently self-funding firms from firms with one lucky cash year. Coverage should exceed the gen-0 version because aqc, a sparsely reported item, is dropped.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( rank( ratio( add( sstk, delta( dltt, 1 ) ), at ) ), rank( ma( ratio( oancf, at ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: GrossCapexVsEarningsInstability
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(capx, MA(dp, 3))), RANK(VOL(RATIO(ib, at), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Capital spending well above the depreciation run-rate means the firm is expanding, not merely maintaining, its capital stock; such expansion is dangerous precisely for firms with unstable earnings, whose managers have the weakest information about the persistence of the demand they are building for.
input_signals.reasoning: Scaling capex by smoothed depreciation is an economically interpretable growth-versus-maintenance measure that is nearly scale-free and available for almost all industrial firms, so coverage should be much higher than the gen-0 signals. Earnings volatility is the quality dimension least captured by FF5's RMW (which is a level, not a second moment), giving this rank-product a better chance of surviving the factor adjustment than the gross-margin-trend version. It is retained as a deliberate product-form control against the mismatch designs above.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( capx, ma( dp, 3 ) ) ), rank( vol( ratio( ib, at ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: RevenuePerCapexDollarTimesCashQuality
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(DELTA(sale, 1), TS_SUM(capx, 3))), RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The realized marginal product of investment — incremental revenue per dollar of cumulative three-year capital spending — identifies firms whose capital budgeting actually works; when this efficiency is paired with strong sustained cash generation, the investment is productive and the market underprices it.
input_signals.reasoning: This flips the search to the long side by measuring investment *output* rather than investment *input*, a construct absent from the archive and only weakly related to CMA (which sorts on input growth). Cumulating capex over three years both matches the lag between spending and revenue and avoids the unstable single-year denominator that would arise from LAG(capx, 1). Pairing with smoothed operating cash flow over assets ensures the revenue gain is converting into cash rather than receivables.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( delta( sale, 1 ), ts_sum( capx, 3 ) ) ), rank( ma( ratio( oancf, at ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: IncrementalGrossProfitPerCapex
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(sale, cogs), 1), TS_SUM(capx, 3))), RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The realized marginal product of capital should be measured in profit, not revenue: incremental gross profit per dollar of cumulative capex identifies firms whose capacity additions earn a spread over cost, and pairing it with sustained cash generation confirms the profit is real.
input_signals.reasoning: This isolates one design choice relative to the archive winner — replacing the revenue numerator with a gross-profit numerator — so a stronger result would show the alpha comes from profitable, not merely voluminous, incremental output. Firms that buy revenue growth at negative margins are demoted rather than promoted, which should sharpen the long leg. Everything else (three-year capex cumulation, cash-flow quality leg) is held fixed for a clean comparison.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( delta( sub( sale, cogs ), 1 ), ts_sum( capx, 3 ) ) ), rank( ma( ratio( oancf, at ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: NetCashSlackTimesProfitability
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at)), RANK(MA(RATIO(ib, at), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Net cash (cash minus total debt) is stored, unexercised investment capacity; when held by persistently profitable firms it represents option value and financing safety that the market underprices, whereas the same slack at unprofitable firms is merely a burn runway.
input_signals.reasoning: This tests the investment theme from the balance-sheet-capacity side rather than the flow side, a genuinely different channel from anything evaluated so far, and it should have very high coverage since cash, debt and income are near-universally reported. The interaction is essential: net cash alone confounds cash-burning biotechs with fortress balance sheets, and profitability alone is RMW. It also gives the batch a low-investment-intensity long side to contrast with the capex-efficiency signals.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( che, add( dltt, dlc ) ), at ) ), rank( ma( ratio( ib, at ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: IndAdjCapexIntoErodingMargins
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppegt)), IND_RANK(NEG(TREND(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), at), 3))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Over-investment into deteriorating unit economics is a within-industry phenomenon: capital intensity and margin levels differ enormously across industries, so an unadjusted sort mostly buys and sells industries, whereas the mispricing lives in the cross-section of peers facing the same technology.
input_signals.reasoning: The gen-0 version had the batch's strongest FMB slope (-3.28) but a zero FF5 alpha and a negative Sharpe, the signature of a portfolio that is long/short industry-level investment and profitability exposure already priced by CMA and RMW. Industry-ranking both legs is the targeted repair for exactly that diagnosis, and shortening the trend window to three years also lifts coverage. If the alpha still fails to appear, we should abandon the input-penalty family entirely.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( capx, ppegt ) ), ind_rank( neg( trend( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), at ), 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: CapexBuildWithDecayingTurnover
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(capx, 3), ppegt)), RANK(NEG(TREND(RATIO(sale, at), 3))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Sustained capacity building while asset turnover is falling means new capital is being added to an already underutilized base; the utilization channel, rather than the margin channel, is where low-quality expansion shows up first and where impairments eventually originate.
input_signals.reasoning: ROA decomposes into margin and turnover, and the archive has only ever crossed investment with the margin/profitability leg; testing the turnover leg tells us which component of quality actually conditions the investment penalty. Cumulative three-year capex over gross PP&E captures a multi-year build rather than a single-year spike, matching the slow horizon over which utilization deteriorates. This is the informative short-side complement to the efficiency signals above.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ts_sum( capx, 3 ), ppegt ) ), rank( neg( trend( ratio( sale, at ), 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: MatchedWindowReturnOnCapex
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(sale, cogs), 3), TS_SUM(capx, 3))), RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The payoff to capital spending accrues over several years, so the correct return-on-investment measure matches a three-year gross-profit gain to the three-year capex outlay that produced it; single-year numerators mismeasure the payoff and add noise.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's best signal used a one-year profit change against a three-year capex sum, a horizon mismatch that understates ROI for firms with long construction lags and overstates it for firms with one good year. Aligning the windows should raise the signal-to-noise ratio of the same economic quantity without changing the mechanism or the coverage, making this a clean test of measurement horizon. The cash-flow conditioning leg is held fixed because it has proven to be the strongest quality dimension.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( delta( sub( sale, cogs ), 3 ), ts_sum( capx, 3 ) ) ), rank( ma( ratio( oancf, at ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: CapexPayoffWithFreeCashFlow
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(sale, cogs), 1), TS_SUM(capx, 3))), RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(oancf, capx), at), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The most convincing evidence of productive investment is profit growth per invested dollar achieved while the firm still generates cash after paying for that investment; free cash flow after capex, not gross operating cash flow, is the quality dimension that certifies investment is self-financing.
input_signals.reasoning: This isolates a single design choice against the archive winner — subtracting capex from operating cash flow in the conditioning leg — which sharpens the distinction between firms that fund growth internally and firms whose gross cash flow is entirely consumed by capex. Because the efficiency leg already rewards low capex, the FCF leg adds financing sustainability rather than double-counting. If it improves both FMB and alpha, self-funding is the operative quality channel.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( delta( sub( sale, cogs ), 1 ), ts_sum( capx, 3 ) ) ), rank( ma( ratio( sub( oancf, capx ), at ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: IssuanceFundedInvestmentNoPayoff
input_signals.expression: SUB(RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, DELTA(dltt, 1)), at)), RANK(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(sale, cogs), 3), TS_SUM(capx, 3))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The worst form of expansion is investment funded by fresh equity and debt issuance that has produced no measurable gross-profit payoff; the wedge between external financing intensity and realized return on invested capital identifies value destruction that neither leg detects alone.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the deliberate short-side construct built from the only two channels in the archive that generated non-trivial alpha — issuance-versus-internal-cash (alpha -2.0%, t=-1.77) and return-on-capex — rather than from the discredited capex-level penalty family. Differencing ranks means both legs of the portfolio contain heavy issuers, so the spread should be driven by the payoff dimension and remain less exposed to CMA. It directly tests whether the ROI mechanism has a symmetric short side.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( rank( ratio( add( sstk, delta( dltt, 1 ) ), at ) ), rank( ratio( delta( sub( sale, cogs ), 3 ), ts_sum( capx, 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: CapexWithFallingDepreciationRate
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(capx, ppegt)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dp, ppent), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms that spend heavily on capital while their recognized depreciation rate on the net capital base falls are stretching asset lives or capitalizing aggressively, inflating current earnings relative to the true cost of the capital being consumed; this accounting-quality-of-investment defect predicts subsequent disappointment.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a distinct channel: rather than asking whether investment is productive, it asks whether the reported cost of investment is honest, a quality dimension entirely absent from the archive and not represented in RMW or CMA. Both inputs are near-universally reported, so coverage should be high, and the interaction is essential because a falling depreciation rate is innocuous for firms that are not investing. It gives the batch a short-side mechanism that is not a repackaged investment level.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( capx, ppegt ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( dp, ppent ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: SlackWithProfitPersistence
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at)), RANK(TS_COUNT(INDICATOR(RATIO(ib, at), 0), 5)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Unexercised investment capacity in the form of net cash is valuable only for firms with a demonstrated record of profitability; counting the number of profitable years over five years separates fortress balance sheets from cash-burning ventures far better than a current profitability level does.
input_signals.reasoning: NetCashSlackTimesProfitability earned a reliable 3.3% alpha but a Sharpe of only 0.115, symptomatic of a long leg polluted by small, currently-profitable-but-fragile cash-rich firms; a five-year persistence count is the natural fix because it demands repeated, not momentary, profitability. Industry-ranking the slack leg further removes the mechanical concentration in cash-heavy sectors that destabilizes the spread. This targets the Sharpe/composition failure mode rather than restating the signal.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( che, add( dltt, dlc ) ), at ) ), rank( ts_count( indicator( ratio( ib, at ), 0 ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: CapitalGrowthSignedByFcfSign
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(GROWTH(ppent, 1)), SIGN(MA(RATIO(SUB(oancf, capx), at), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Capacity expansion is rewarded when the firm is a persistent net cash generator after investment and punished when it is a persistent cash consumer; the sign of sustained free cash flow, not its magnitude, is the switch that determines whether growth is productive or fragile.
input_signals.reasoning: Because SIGN reduces the quality leg to a binary switch, both the long and short extremes are populated by high-PP&E-growth firms, so the spread cannot be a repackaged FCF-profitability or CMA sort — it is the interaction itself. If this retains most of SelfFundedCapitalStockGrowth's 5.6% alpha, the mechanism is genuinely conditional; if it collapses, the archive winner was largely a single-theme cash-profitability effect, which is the single most important diagnostic left to run.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( ppent, 1 ) ), sign( ma( ratio( sub( oancf, capx ), at ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: ExternalFinanceMinusInternalFunds
input_signals.expression: SUB(RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, DELTA(dltt, 1)), at)), RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), capx), at), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms whose expansion is financed by security issuance while their internal funds fall short of their own capital spending are the low-quality expanders; the ranked wedge between external financing intensity and internal self-funding capacity is the cleanest short-side statement of the theme.
input_signals.reasoning: It upgrades the archive's strongest short-side construct by replacing the payoff leg (three-year gross-profit change per capex dollar) with the funding-capacity leg that has proven to be the more powerful quality dimension, and by using ib+dp it should materially exceed the 0.096 coverage of the prior version. Both portfolio legs still contain issuers and non-issuers ranked against internal funding, so the spread should stay orthogonal to CMA. This tests whether the FCF channel has the symmetric short side that capex-level penalties never had.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( rank( ratio( add( sstk, delta( dltt, 1 ) ), at ) ), rank( ma( ratio( sub( add( ib, dp ), capx ), at ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: SelfFundedGrowthPlusCapexPayoff
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(MUL(RANK(GROWTH(ppent, 1)), RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(oancf, capx), at), 3))), RATIO(DELTA(SUB(sale, cogs), 3), TS_SUM(capx, 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Self-funded expansion and realized profit payoff per invested dollar are complementary pieces of evidence about investment quality — the first is about financing discipline, the second about operating outcome — so a firm scoring high on both is the most reliable productive investor.
input_signals.reasoning: The two strongest archive mechanisms use different information (funding sufficiency versus realized ROI) and correlate imperfectly, so ranking them together should reduce idiosyncratic measurement noise and lift the t-statistics of both the FMB slope and the alpha without introducing a new economic assumption. SUMRANK is used rather than multiplication so that a firm strong on one dimension is not zeroed out by a mediocre score on the other. This is the batch's consolidation candidate for the remaining generations.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( mul( rank( growth( ppent, 1 ) ), rank( ma( ratio( sub( oancf, capx ), at ), 3 ) ) ), ratio( delta( sub( sale, cogs ), 3 ), ts_sum( capx, 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: GrowthWithUninterruptedPositiveFcf
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(GROWTH(ppent, 1)), SIGN(TS_MIN(SUB(oancf, capx), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: What certifies expansion is not average free cash flow but never having needed outside money: firms that generated positive free cash flow in every one of the last three years are demonstrably self-funding, and their capacity growth should be rewarded rather than penalized.
input_signals.reasoning: This tightens the winning binary switch from "average FCF positive" to "minimum FCF positive," which removes firms whose three-year mean is rescued by one exceptional year — precisely the marginal cases most likely to blur the long and short legs. The two-sided structure that produced the archive's best Sharpe is preserved, so any improvement is attributable to a cleaner definition of self-funding. It is a single, economically motivated design change rather than a new formula family.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( ppent, 1 ) ), sign( ts_min( sub( oancf, capx ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: AssetGrowthSignedByFcfSign
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(GROWTH(at, 1)), SIGN(MA(RATIO(SUB(oancf, capx), at), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The asset-growth anomaly is entirely a low-quality-expansion phenomenon: total asset growth predicts low returns among cash-consuming firms and non-negative or positive returns among persistently self-funding firms, so the same growth measure carries opposite information in the two regimes.
input_signals.reasoning: This applies the validated sign-switch to the broadest and most heavily documented investment measure — total asset growth, which includes acquisitions, working capital and financial assets, not just PP&E — making it the most direct test of the theme's central claim. Because CMA sorts on unconditional asset growth, a positive alpha here would show the factor is mixing two economically opposite populations. Coverage should be at least as good as the PP&E version since asset growth needs no capital-expenditure detail.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( at, 1 ) ), sign( ma( ratio( sub( oancf, capx ), at ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: IssuanceGrowthByCashBurners
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, DELTA(dltt, 1)), at)), NEG(SIGN(MA(RATIO(SUB(oancf, capx), at), 3))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Security issuance is benign for firms that already fund their own investment and toxic for firms that do not; the interaction of external financing intensity with a persistent free-cash-flow deficit identifies the expansion the market should discount most heavily.
input_signals.reasoning: The short side has so far only worked through rank differences (best alpha −2.2%), while the sign-switch structure has proven far more effective at isolating interactions; this transplants that structure to the financing channel so that heavy issuers appear in both legs, separated only by cash sufficiency. It also repairs the gen-4 failure in which the ib+dp proxy flipped the same construct's alpha positive by returning to cash-flow-statement measurement. If it works, we have a matched long/short pair built on one mechanism.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( add( sstk, delta( dltt, 1 ) ), at ) ), neg( sign( ma( ratio( sub( oancf, capx ), at ), 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: GrowthWithCashBackedEarnings
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(GROWTH(ppent, 1)), SUMRANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(oancf, capx), at), 3), NEG(MA(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 3))))
input_signals.hypothesis: High-quality expansion requires both that investment be internally funded and that reported earnings be backed by cash rather than accruals; growth financed from cash flow but accompanied by large positive accruals is a warning that the cash flow itself is being managed.
input_signals.reasoning: The gen-4 result that ib+dp destroyed the signal implies the accrual component of earnings carries the quality information, so this makes accrual quality an explicit second conditioning channel via SUMRANK rather than leaving it implicit in oancf. Using SUMRANK rather than a triple product avoids zeroing out firms that are strong on one dimension and keeps the composite well spread. This directly tests the interpretation of the batch's most informative failure.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( ppent, 1 ) ), sumrank( ma( ratio( sub( oancf, capx ), at ), 3 ), neg( ma( ratio( sub( ib, oancf ), at ), 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: OwnHistoryCapexBurstSelfFunded
input_signals.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5), SIGN(MA(RATIO(SUB(oancf, capx), at), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters is investment relative to the firm's own recent norm, not relative to other firms: a capital-spending burst above a firm's five-year history signals a deliberate new investment cycle, which is value-creating when the firm funds it internally and value-destroying when it does not.
input_signals.reasoning: Cross-sectional capex ranks are dominated by permanent industry capital intensity, which is why capex-level designs kept producing factor-clone spreads; a within-firm time-series rank strips that out and measures the decision to accelerate investment. Pairing it with the validated FCF sign switch keeps the interaction two-sided and tests whether the mechanism is about investment *changes* rather than investment *levels*. This is a structurally different investment measure from anything in the archive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ts_rank( ratio( capx, ppent ), 5 ), sign( ma( ratio( sub( oancf, capx ), at ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: AssetGrowthWithCashBackedFunding
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(GROWTH(at, 1)), SUMRANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(oancf, capx), at), 3), NEG(MA(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 3))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Expansion is high quality when it is both funded from free cash flow and accompanied by earnings that convert into cash; total asset growth crossed with this two-channel quality score should separate productive expanders from firms growing on external money and accruals.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the direct consolidation of the archive's two strongest results — the broader asset-growth leg that raised FMB to 3.03 and alpha to 5.3%, and the FCF-plus-accrual SUMRANK quality leg that raised FMB to 3.46 — neither of which has been combined. Because the two quality channels are imperfectly correlated, the composite should reduce measurement noise and lift both the slope and the alpha t-statistic rather than merely restating either parent. It is the leading candidate for the final signal.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( at, 1 ) ), sumrank( ma( ratio( sub( oancf, capx ), at ), 3 ), neg( ma( ratio( sub( ib, oancf ), at ), 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AssetGrowthWithSolvencyAndCashQuality
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(GROWTH(at, 1)), SUMRANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(oancf, capx), at), 3), SUMRANK(NEG(MA(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 3)), NEG(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Fragility has a stock dimension as well as a flow dimension: expansion by firms that are self-funding, cash-backed and lightly levered is the highest-quality growth, while leverage marks the firms for whom an investment program becomes a solvency problem.
input_signals.reasoning: Debt-service capacity showed a genuine but weak standalone effect (alpha 3.4%, t=2.47, FMB 0.90), suggesting leverage is informative but noisy on its own; nesting it as a third ranked channel tests whether it adds incrementally to the flow-based quality score rather than competing with it. If the three-channel version beats signal 1, the theme's "fragile firms" story needs a balance-sheet component; if not, we learn the mechanism is purely about cash flows. Leverage is measured as a simple level to avoid adding estimation windows that would cost coverage.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( at, 1 ) ), sumrank( ma( ratio( sub( oancf, capx ), at ), 3 ), sumrank( neg( ma( ratio( sub( ib, oancf ), at ), 3 ) ), neg( ratio( add( dltt, dlc ), at ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AssetGrowthSwitchedByCashVsAccruals
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(GROWTH(at, 1)), SIGN(SUB(MA(RATIO(SUB(oancf, capx), at), 3), MA(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 3))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The regime that determines whether growth is good or bad is whether sustained free cash flow exceeds sustained accruals: firms whose cash generation dominates their accrual accumulation can expand safely, while firms in the opposite regime are growing on paper earnings.
input_signals.reasoning: The binary-switch structure gave the archive's best Sharpe ratios (0.52–0.56) because both portfolio legs contain high-growth firms, making the spread nearly orthogonal to CMA; here the switch is upgraded from FCF sign alone to a comparison of the two quality channels that matter.
